blocks.text: Guarantee that a scope holds exactly one instance of a class, and give it a well-known access point.

The classic form uses a private constructor and a static accessor, making the instance **global**. Modern Java gets the guarantee from an **enum** or from a **DI container's singleton scope**, which keeps the one-instance rule without hiding a global dependency.

items: **Guarantees:** one instance per class loader or container.
**Costs:** global state, hidden dependencies, harder tests.
**Better form:** one instance, passed in, not looked up.

blocks.text: Singleton is the most overused pattern. Often you need one instance by choice, which is a wiring decision, not a class-level rule.

walkthrough.note: An enum constant is the simplest correct singleton. The JVM guarantees one instance, thread-safe creation, and protection from reflection and serialization attacks.

Lazy and lock-free: `Holder` initializes on the first `get()`, and the JVM makes class initialization thread-safe. Unlike the enum, reflection can still call the constructor, and `Serializable` would need `readResolve`.
Each call reaches the same `AtomicLong`, so the numbers increase across call sites without synchronization.
Nothing is created before first use, the two references are identical, and the constructor ran exactly once.

blocks.text: A shared metrics registry in a server application.

Counters and timers from every component must land in one registry that a scrape endpoint reads. Instead of a static accessor, the application creates a single `MetricRegistry` at startup and the container injects it into each component. There is still one instance, but tests can pass a fresh one and no class reaches out to a global.
Payoff: one shared instance without a global, so tests and parallel runs stay isolated.

lists.title: Use when
items: Exactly one instance is required by the domain, such as a hardware handle or a JVM-wide cache.
A container manages the single instance and you inject it.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: You only want to share an object; pass it as a dependency instead.
Tests need to replace it, which a static accessor makes hard.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Hidden dependencies: any code can call `get()` and become coupled to it.
Mutable singletons are shared state that needs explicit thread safety.
Hand-written double-checked locking without `volatile` is broken.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Every service reaches `X.getInstance()` instead of receiving X.
A singleton holding per-request or per-user data.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Use an enum when you need a true language-level singleton.
Otherwise prefer the container's singleton scope; one instance per container, injected.

rows.difference: Injection gives you one shared instance without making it global. The one-instance rule lives in wiring, so tests can substitute it.
Both are global access points. A locator looks up many services by key; a singleton exposes exactly one, and both hide dependencies.
A singleton is one instance of a whole class. Flyweight shares many small immutable instances, one per distinct value.
Concrete factories are usually stateless, so one instance per application is enough and is often held as a singleton.
Lazy singletons were the original reason for this idiom; the holder class and enums make it unnecessary in Java.

Flyweight keeps a pool of many shared instances keyed by value, not one instance of the whole class.

exercises.scenario: A desktop tool talks to one physical hardware dongle. Only one connection may exist per process, many unrelated components need it, and the tool runs without a DI container.

options.why: The domain demands exactly one instance, and with no container a guarded static access point is the pragmatic way to provide it.
It would be preferable, but here there is no container to wire the instance, so a class-level guarantee is what enforces the rule.
Copying would create a second connection to the device, which is the one thing that must not happen.
Flyweight shares many small immutable values; this is a single stateful connection.

exercises.prompt: Explain Singleton in your own words: what does it guarantee, and why is it often a poor choice?

modelAnswer.text: Singleton guarantees one instance in a scope and exposes it globally. The global access hides dependencies and makes testing and parallel runs hard. Prefer one instance held by a DI container and injected, or an enum when a true language-level singleton is needed.

keyPoints: One instance per class loader, enforced by the class
Global access hides dependencies and hurts tests
Enum or holder idiom are the safe forms
Lazy init without synchronization is a race
